Clinical Features
Rupture of a tubal pregnancy is a medical emergency. The clinical
course of ectopic tubal pregnancy is characterized by the onset of mod-
erate to severe abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding 6 to 8 weeks after
the last menstrual period, correlating with distention and then rupture
of the fallopian tube. In such cases, the patient may rapidly develop
hemorrhagic shock and signs of an acute abdomen. Rapid diagnosis is
critical and is based on determination of inappropriately rising chori-
onic  gonadotropin  titers,  pelvic  sonography,  endometrial  biopsy
(which shows decidua without chorionic villi, trophoblast, or placental
implantation site), and/or laparoscopy. Despite advances in early diag-
nosis and treatment, ectopic pregnancy still accounts for 4% to 10% of
pregnancy-related deaths.
DISORDERS OF MID TO LATE SECOND TRIMESTER
GESTATIONS
During the second trimester, fetal nutritional demands increase rapidly,
and therefore disorders of the placenta take on increased importance.
This is also the stage of fetal development during which congenital
malformations take an increasing toll (Chapter 10). In severe cases,
disorders that are more typical of third trimester gestations (discussed
next), such as infections (e.g., amniotic fluid infection: acute chorioam-
nionitis, and viral infections as in CMV) and placental hypoplasia, may
appear during the second trimester. When they do so, they are more
likely to lead to fetal demise because the immature placenta has less
reserve capacity for nutrient exchange. Another cause of second trimes-
ter loss are disorders causing diminished perfusion of the fetal side of
the placental circulation. These are poorly understood but are marked
morphologically by the presence of villous vascular thrombi and endo-
thelial damage, or avascular villi.
DISORDERS OF THE THIRD TRIMESTER,
PERIPARTUM, AND PUERPERIUM
In the third trimester, umbilical cord pathologies play a major role in
poor pregnancy outcome. Interruption of blood flow through the um-
bilical cord from any cause (e.g., constricting knots (Fig. 22.47A), kinks,
nuchal or body cords, prolapse or other causes of compression) causes
significant morbidity and is often fatal. Acute umbilical cord obstruction
associated with fetal demise leaves few morphologic clues, but chronic or
intermittent interruption of blood flow leads to characteristic placental
changes  of  fetal  vascular  malperfusion  (such  as  avascular  villi
(Fig. 22.47B) or vascular thrombi). Other disorders of this period include
complications related to twin pregnancies, maternal vascular malperfu-
sion, abnormal placental implantation, and infections.
Fig. 22.47 Examples of pathologies associated with fetal vascular malper-
fusion. (A) Tight complex true knot of the umbilical cord. Occlusion of the
umbilical vessels by the knot leads to downstream villous fetal vascular
malperfusion. (B) Avascular villi caused by malperfusion. Compare with
normally vascularized villi (bottom left) to the avascular villi (top right).
Twin Placentas
Twin pregnancies arise from fertilization of two ova (dizygotic) or
from division of one fertilized ovum (monozygotic). There are three
types of twin placentas (Fig. 22.48): diamnionic dichorionic (which
may be fused or separate); diamnionic monochorionic; and monoam-
nionic monochorionic. Monochorionic placentas imply monozygotic
(identical) twins, and the time at which splitting of the developing
embryo occurs determines whether there is a dividing membrane and
two amnions or no dividing membrane. Dichorionic placentation may
occur with either monozygotic or dizygotic twins.
Multiple gestations carry many risks, and twins may be discordant
for size, karyotype, malformations, and placental pathologies. One
unique  complication  of  monochorionic  twin  pregnancy  is  twin-
to-twin  transfusion  syndrome.  Monochorionic  twin  placentas  have
vascular anastomoses that connect the twin circulations. Twin-to-twin
perfusion syndrome results when these shunts preferentially increase
blood flow to one twin at the expense of the second, causing one twin
(the donor) to be under perfused and the second twin (the recipient)
to be fluid overloaded. If severe, it may result in the death of one or
both fetuses.
Maternal Vascular Malperfusion
Maternal vascular malperfusion refers to inadequate blood supply to the
intervillous space due to various abnormalities in the maternal circula-
tion of the placenta. It may be precipitated by abnormal placental im-
plantation or development, or maternal vascular disease; the effects
range from mild intrauterine growth restriction to severe uteroplacental

• Failure of the normal physiologic remodeling of the placental bed vessels. The precipitating events in preeclampsia are abnormally shallow
trophoblastic implantation and a failure of physiologic remodeling of
the maternal vessels, which is required for adequate perfusion of the
placenta. At the implantation site of a normal pregnancy, fetal
extravillous trophoblast invade the maternal decidua and decidual
vessels, destroy the vascular smooth muscle, and replace the maternal endothelial cells with fetal trophoblastic cells, forming hybrid
fetomaternal blood vessels. This process converts the decidual spiral
arteries from small-caliber resistance vessels to large-capacity
low-resistance uteroplacental vessels lacking a smooth muscle coat
(Fig. 22.51). In preeclampsia, this vascular remodeling fails to occur,
leaving the placenta ill equipped to meet the increased circulatory
demands of late gestation and setting the stage for the development
of placental ischemia.
• Endothelial dysfunction and imbalance of angiogenic and antiangiogenic factors. It is postulated that in response to hypoxia, the ischemic placenta releases factors into the maternal circulation that
cause an imbalance in circulating angiogenic and anti-angiogenic
factors; this, in turn, leads to systemic maternal endothelial
dysfunction and the clinical manifestations of the disease. In support of this, the blood levels of two placenta-derived antiangiogenic
factors, soluble feline McDonough sarcoma (FMS)-like tyrosine
kinase (sFLT-1) and endoglin, which antagonize the effects of
VEGF and TGFb, respectively, are several orders of magnitude
higher in females with preeclampsia than in healthy controls. In
preeclampsia, high levels of sFlt1 and soluble endoglin bring about
a decrease in angiogenesis much earlier than in normal pregnancy,
resulting in defective placental vascular development. Furthermore, TGFb induces endothelial production of nitric oxide, a potent vasodilator; thus, inhibition of TGFb by endoglin may directly
contribute to systemic vasoconstriction, hypertension, and tissue
hypoperfusion. Studies in animal models also implicate sFlt l and
soluble endoglin in the pathogenesis of endothelial dysfunction.
When sFLT1 and endoglin are overexpressed together, pregnant
rats develop nephrotic-range proteinuria, severe hypertension, as
well as features of the HELLP syndrome, including elevated liver
enzymes, decreased platelet count, and hemolysis, while their pups
are growth restricted, all hallmarks of severe preeclampsia. Thus, it
seems that sFlt1 and soluble endoglin are key mediators that link
the placenta to the characteristic maternal endothelial dysfunction
of preeclampsia.

and capillaries throughout the body, but particularly in the placenta,

Clinical Features
Preeclampsia/eclampsia is an important cause of maternal and fetal
mortality worldwide due to hypertensive crises, strokes, and abnormal
bleeding due to disseminated intravascular coagulation. Preeclampsia
most commonly occurs after 34 weeks of gestation but begins earlier in
females  with  hydatidiform  mole  (discussed  later)  or  preexisting
kidney disease, hypertension, or coagulopathies. The onset is typically
marked by hypertension and edema, with proteinuria appearing several
days  later.  Headaches  and  visual  disturbances  may  follow  and  are
indicative of preeclampsia with severe features, often requiring early
delivery. Eclampsia is heralded by more severe central nervous system
involvement, including seizures, eventual coma, and even death.
Management of preeclampsia differs depending on the gestational
age and severity of disease. For term pregnancies, delivery is the treat-
ment of choice regardless of disease severity. For preterm pregnancies in
which delivery place the fetus at risk, mild disease can be managed ex-
pectantly by controlling maternal hypertension and by close monitoring
of the mother and fetus. However, eclampsia, preeclampsia with severe
features, fetal compromise, or the HELLP syndrome are indications for
delivery regardless of gestational age.
Following delivery, proteinuria and hypertension usually disappear
within 1 to 2 weeks later. Although in most instances preeclampsia has
no lasting sequelae, about 20% of affected females develop hypertension
and microalbuminuria within 7 years of a pregnancy complicated by
preeclampsia. There is also a two-fold increase in the long-term risk of
cardiovascular disease.

Partial moles result from fertilization of an egg with two sperm

oval with central cavitation (cisterns) and are covered by a trophoblast prolifera-

inclusions (Fig. 22.55).

Hydatidiform Mole
Hydatidiform moles are important to recognize because they are associated with an increased risk of persistent trophoblastic disease

(invasive mole) or choriocarcinoma. Moles are characterized histologically by cystic swelling of the chorionic villi and circumferential biphasic trophoblastic hyperplasia. They are usually diagnosed during early pregnancy (average 9 weeks) by pelvic sonography. Molar pregnancy can develop at any age, but the risk is higher at the two ends of reproductive life, during puberty and in perimenopausal females. For unknown reasons, the incidence varies considerably in different parts of the world. Hydatidiform mole occurs in about 1 in 1000 to 2000 pregnancies in the United States, but it is twice as common in Southeast Asia. Two types of noninvasive moles—complete and partial—can be identified by cytogenetic and histologic studies.
Complete Mole

Complete mole results from fertilization of an egg that has lost (or subsequently loses) its female chromosomes, and as a result its nuclear genetic material is completely paternally derived. Ninety percent have a diploid 46,XX karyotype stemming from duplication of the genetic material of one sperm (a phenomenon called androgenesis that produces monospermic complete hydatidiform mole) (Fig. 22.53A). The remaining 10% result from the fertilization of an “empty” egg by two sperm (dispermic complete hydatidiform mole) (Fig. 22.53B); these may have a 46,XX or 46,XY karyotype. In complete moles, there is no embryonic development. Patients have 2.5% risk of subsequent choriocarcinoma and a 15% risk of persistent or invasive mole.
Partial Mole
Partial moles result from fertilization of an egg with two sperm

(Fig. 22.53C). In these moles, the karyotype is triploid (e.g., 69,XXY) or  occasionally  tetraploid  (92,XXXY).  Fetal  development  may be seen, but the fetus is characteristically growth restricted and has lethal anomalies of the central nervous system as well as skeletal abnormalities such as syndactyly. Partial moles have an increased risk of persistent molar disease but are not typically associated with postmolar choriocarcinoma.
MORPHOLOGY
Grossly, classic hydatidiform moles appear as a delicate, friable mass of thin-walled
, translucent, cystic, grapelike structures consisting of swollen edematous

(hydropic) villi (Fig. 22.54A). In complete mole, the microscopic abnormalities involve all or most of the villous tissue. The chorionic villi are enlarged, smooth and oval with central cavitation (cisterns) and are covered by a trophoblast proliferation that includes both cytotrophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts (Fig. 22.54B).

In contrast, in partial moles, only a fraction of the villi is enlarged and edematous, the trophoblastic hyperplasia is focal and less marked, and only syncytiotrophoblasts are hyperplastic. Partial moles have irregular villous outlines, unlike the smooth round outlines of a complete mole, often with prominent trophoblastic inclusions (Fig. 22.55).

Invasive mole is an infiltrative lesion that penetrates and sometimes perforates the uterine wall. Tumors of Extravascular Trophoblasts

Two uncommon malignant tumors of extravascular trophoblasts have unique biologic and morphologic features and merit brief mention.
